stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians have often cited dye analyses of surviving seventeenth-century Dutch woolens as evidence that blue was the period's most popular color for everyday clothing: nearly 60 percent of the tested fragments contain indigo or woad. However, those blue dyes bind to wool far more stably than the era's weld-based yellows and madder-based reds, which fade and wash out over decades of wear. The high share of blue among the fragments therefore ______
choices: shows that red and yellow woolens were in fact more common than blue ones during the period.
may reflect which dyes endured over time rather than which colors people most often chose to wear.
indicates that seventeenth-century dyers favored indigo because it held up better than other dyes.
suggests that dye analysis cannot identify the plant sources used in faded wool fragments.
explanation: The problem is a survival bias. Blue dyes last, and reds and yellows fade away, so the fragments that still show color are skewed toward blue. That makes the link between 'what survives' and 'what people wore' uncertain. It doesn't show that any other color was more popular. Choice B states only that uncertainty.

A.why: You treated the complication as proof of the opposite. Fading dyes make the blue share unreliable, but nothing shows red or yellow was actually more common.

C.why: You added a step that isn't in the passage. The text says blue dyes last longer on surviving cloth. It says nothing about why dyers chose them or whether they knew this.

D.why: You focused on the lab method instead of what the 60 percent figure can show. The passage never says analysis fails on faded fragments. Its point is about which colors survived.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a survey of 3,000 adults, those who reported eating the most added sugar had, on average, lower body mass indexes than those who reported eating the least. Intake was measured with a single 24-hour dietary recall, however, and validation studies have found that adults with higher body mass indexes tend to underreport sugary foods more than other adults do. The survey's finding therefore ______
choices: indicates that a single 24-hour recall is the most common way researchers measure diet.
shows that higher-BMI adults underreport sugar because they are trying to lose weight.
may stem partly from differences in reporting accuracy rather than in what people actually ate.
demonstrates that lower-BMI adults actually consume more added sugar than other adults do.
explanation: The problem is that one group underreports more than the others. If higher-BMI adults leave out more sugary foods, their reported intake looks lower than it really is, and that alone could produce the pattern. So the finding might not reflect real differences in diet. Choice C says exactly that and claims nothing firmer.

A.why: You grabbed a detail about the method. The passage never says how common the recall method is, and that doesn't explain what the flaw means for the finding.

B.why: You supplied a cause the passage never gives. The text says higher-BMI adults underreport more. It doesn't say why.

D.why: You trusted the reported numbers even though the passage just gave you a reason to doubt them. Biased reporting makes the pattern uncertain, so it can't confirm a firm claim about actual intake.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers testing a new concrete mix subjected sample slabs to 300 freeze-thaw cycles, after which the slabs showed less surface scaling than slabs of conventional concrete did. The test slabs were frozen in plain water, however, while most highway pavement in cold regions is also exposed to de-icing salts, which can greatly accelerate scaling in some mixes. The test results therefore ______
choices: may not accurately predict how the new mix will perform on highways that are routinely salted.
show that the new mix will scale faster than conventional concrete once it is exposed to salt.
indicate that de-icing salts damage the new mix more severely than plain freezing water does.
show that the new mix scaled more than conventional concrete did under freeze-thaw cycling.
explanation: The flaw is that the test left out salt, which real roads face and which speeds up scaling in some mixes. That weakens the link between the lab result and how the mix will do on the road. It doesn't show how the mix will actually behave with salt. Choice A says only that the prediction may not hold.

B.why: You turned a gap in the test into a firm prediction that the mix will fail. Salt wasn't tested, so the result is unknown, not negative.

C.why: You missed the word 'some.' Salt speeds up scaling in some mixes, and the passage never says the new mix is one of them.

D.why: You reversed the reported result. The passage says the new mix scaled less than conventional concrete.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: After a school district launched a handwashing campaign, officials credited it with a 20 percent drop in illness-related absences compared with the previous winter. Yet national surveillance data show that the influenza season that winter was among the mildest in a decade, with infection rates down sharply even in regions without such campaigns. The decline in absences therefore ______
choices: shows that the campaign had no measurable effect on the spread of illness in the district.
suggests that handwashing campaigns work best during unusually mild influenza seasons.
was unusual, since illness rates rose that winter in regions without such campaigns.
could have occurred even if the campaign had done little to reduce illness among students.
explanation: The confound is the mild flu season, which cut illness everywhere, including places with no campaign. That means the drop might have happened anyway, so you can't credit it to the campaign with confidence. It doesn't prove the campaign failed either. Choice D keeps to that limit.

A.why: You treated another possible explanation as proof that the campaign did nothing. The mild season makes the campaign's effect uncertain. It doesn't rule the campaign out.

B.why: You drew a new general rule from one district in one season. Nothing in the passage compares how campaigns work in mild seasons versus severe ones.

C.why: You reversed the national data. The passage says infection rates fell sharply in regions without campaigns.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Comparing a 1712 nautical chart of a stretch of the Normandy coast with modern satellite imagery, a geographer found that the charted shoreline lies about 400 meters seaward of today's. The 1712 surveyors, however, fixed coastal positions from offshore vessels by estimating distances by eye, a method that historians of cartography say routinely produced errors of several hundred meters. The apparent difference between the two shorelines therefore ______
choices: proves that the coast has eroded far less since 1712 than the comparison implies.
may be due as much to the limits of the early survey as to any actual erosion.
shows that the 1712 surveyors placed every coastal feature too far out to sea.
indicates that satellite imagery is less precise than estimating distances by eye.
explanation: The problem is that the old survey's errors were about as large as the gap being measured. So the 400 meters could be real erosion, survey error, or both. Choice B says the difference may come from the survey's limits. It doesn't claim to know how much erosion actually happened.

A.why: You took 'the chart may be wrong' to mean 'erosion was small.' Errors could go either way, so the true amount of erosion is unknown, not proven smaller.

C.why: You assumed the errors all pointed the same way and applied that to every feature. The passage gives only their size, 'several hundred meters,' not their direction.

D.why: You reversed the comparison. The passage presents estimating by eye as the error-prone method and treats the satellite imagery as the reliable baseline.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because living floras in warm climates have a higher proportion of species with smooth-edged leaves, paleobotanists often estimate ancient temperatures from the share of smooth-edged leaves in a fossil assemblage. At one Eocene site in Wyoming, only 30 percent of the fossil leaf types are smooth-edged, implying a cool climate. But the fossils come from former streambank deposits, and streamside plants tend to have toothed leaves even in warm regions. The site's low share of smooth-edged leaves therefore ______
choices: demonstrates that the Wyoming region was warm rather than cool during the Eocene.
confirms that streamside plants mostly had smooth-edged leaves during the Eocene.
might reflect the plants' wet habitat more than the region's actual temperatures.
indicates that leaf-margin analysis cannot be applied to any fossil assemblage.
explanation: The flaw is the sample. Streamside plants have toothed leaves even when the climate is warm, so a streambank collection could make the climate look cooler than it was. That breaks the link between leaf shape and temperature at this site. It doesn't tell you what the temperature actually was. Choice C names only that uncertainty.

A.why: You flipped the conclusion to its opposite. The streambank bias makes the 'cool' estimate unreliable, but no evidence here shows the region was warm.

B.why: You reversed the key fact. The passage says streamside plants tend to have toothed leaves, not smooth-edged ones.

D.why: You stretched one site's problem to every fossil collection. The flaw applies to streambank deposits like this one, not to the method in general.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some seismologists have proposed that an earthquake that struck the region in 1787 was among the largest in its recorded history, citing colonial accounts describing widespread building collapses across dozens of settlements. However, most structures in those settlements were built of unreinforced adobe, which can collapse under shaking far weaker than masonry or timber buildings withstand. The extent of the reported damage therefore ______
choices: shows that the 1787 earthquake was smaller than any other in the region's history.
indicates that the colonial accounts exaggerated how many buildings had collapsed.
reveals why settlers in the region preferred adobe to masonry or timber construction.
could suggest a larger quake than occurred even if the colonial accounts are accurate.
explanation: The complication is fragile buildings. Adobe falls down under modest shaking, so heavy damage doesn't have to mean a huge quake. That makes the jump from damage to magnitude uncertain, even if every account is true. Choice D says the damage could overstate the quake's size. It doesn't claim the quake was small.

A.why: You replaced one firm claim with an even stronger opposite one. Fragile buildings make 'largest' doubtful, but they can't rank the quake as the smallest.

B.why: You doubted the wrong thing. The passage doesn't question how accurate the accounts are. It questions what the damage they describe says about magnitude.

C.why: You followed a side detail about building materials. The passage never explains why settlers chose adobe, and that doesn't address what the damage shows.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In a trial of a beetroot-juice supplement, 24 recreational runners completed a 5-kilometer time trial after drinking either the juice or plain water, and their times were on average 2 percent faster after the juice. Because the juice's color and taste are unmistakable, however, every runner knew which drink they had received, and athletes who expect a performance aid to work often push harder. The faster times therefore ______
choices: may owe something to the runners' expectations rather than to the juice itself.
prove that the juice's benefit came entirely from the runners' expectations.
indicate that the juice would give elite runners a similar 2 percent benefit.
show that the runners pushed harder after drinking water than after the juice.
explanation: The flaw is that the trial wasn't blind. Runners knew which drink they had, and expecting a boost can make athletes push harder. That means some of the improvement might come from expectation rather than from the juice. Choice A raises that possibility without claiming to know how much of the effect is real.

B.why: You changed 'might partly explain' into 'fully explains.' The passage raises expectation as a possible factor. It doesn't rule out a real effect from the juice.

C.why: You applied a small study of recreational runners to elite athletes, a group the trial never tested.

D.why: You reversed the expectation effect. Runners who expect a boost push harder after the supplement, not after the water.
